text: A Data Policy is a record on sys_data_policy2, scoped to a table, just like a UI Policy is scoped to a table. But the difference is where the rule actually gets enforced. A UI Policy's rule lives entirely in the browser and only fires when that specific form renders. A Data Policy's rule is enforced by the platform itself, on the server, at the exact moment a record is written — and it genuinely does not matter which door that write came through. If the rule says a field must be filled in, the platform refuses to save the record without it, whether that save comes from a user clicking Submit, an overnight Import Set, a REST API call, or an admin running a background script.

Just like a UI Policy delegates its real work to UI Policy Actions, a Data Policy delegates its real work to child records on sys_data_policy_rule. Each rule names one field on the governed table and sets one of exactly two enforcement options: Mandatory, meaning the field must have a value before the record saves through any write path, or Read-only, meaning the field can't be changed by that write path once the record exists. A Data Policy also carries a condition — the rule only applies when that condition evaluates true for the record being saved, exactly the same shape as 'Business Justification is mandatory, but only when Priority is 1 dash Critical.'

Data Policies have one more useful setting worth knowing: Apply to UI. When checked, the platform doesn't just enforce the rule on save — it also pushes that same mandatory or read-only behavior onto the form, so the end user sees the field marked mandatory before they even try to submit. This is why many admins think of a Data Policy as the more complete version of a mandatory or read-only rule. One thing it still can't do: Apply to UI never adds Visible behavior — a field that needs to be hidden or revealed still needs an actual UI Policy.

Recall last lesson's scenario: Asset Tag marked mandatory by a UI Policy, but a REST API call creates a Hardware incident with Asset Tag left blank, and the record saves anyway, because the UI Policy never evaluates outside the form. A Data Policy with that identical condition and rule closes the gap completely. The same API call now gets rejected by the platform itself, with no form, no browser, and no UI Policy involved.

Server-side, write-path-agnostic enforcement is the whole point of this mechanism, and it's what separates it from everything Lesson 20 could offer. Next up: the real decision point administrators actually face day to day — when a UI Policy alone is genuinely enough, and when a Data Policy is the only honest answer.
